Meeting header:
Date: 2026-12-29

Attendees: Jordan Li, Samira Patel, Diego Alvarez (Redwood) -- Alex Monroe, Priya Shah, Marcus Lee, Tara Nguyen (LumenHealth)

Summary: Short technical workshop to diagnose observed production stalls when the customer's DNS resolvers intermittently return NXDOMAIN or slow responses; align on mitigations (circuit-breaker, host caching, PrivateLink routing) and reproduce tests.

Topics: NAT Egress, PrivateLink, DNS caching, KV cache warm-up, batching latency, quantization trade-offs

Transcript body:
[00:00:00] Jordan: hey everyone, uh thanks for joining. we've got about an hour and change, uh we'll try to focus on the DNS stalls you saw in prod and how that interacts with kv cache warm up and our batching behavior. Samira, wanna intro the repro?
[00:00:15] Samira: yeah sure. so Marcus flagged that during peak window they see 200–300ms tail latencies jump to multiple seconds and occasionally requests time out. logs show repeated DNS timeouts to the egress resolver and then retries. so the runtime stalls waiting for name resolution for various external resources, like mirrors and occasionally for metrics endpoints.
[00:00:40] Marcus: yeah and just to add, it's not every request; it's intermittent but spikes correlate with NAT gateway scale events and with resolver health changes. we also saw cross-az differences — us-east-1a had higher failures.
[00:00:55] Tara: question — we use a pair of VPC resolvers in each AZ, they're forwarded to an internal resolver fleet. sometimes the forwarders hit a throttle because of firewall rules, not sure.
[00:01:10] Diego: right and one pattern we see is "hairpinning" where egress goes out and back in which can change source IP and break split-horizon DNS. that leads to a resolved IP that is valid but points to an unhealthy AZ. the runtime then follows that IP and that connection stalls.
[00:01:30] Alex: yup and the retry behavior in the client ends up queuing more requests because of our batching window, so one stalled connection increases tail latency across the worker.
[00:01:45] Samira: exactly; batching helps throughput but it amplifies tail latency when a single token generation holds the KV cache or the worker thread. we suggested smaller max batch at low p99 SLOs, but the root cause here is DNS + egress routing.
[00:02:05] Priya: security-level question — we can't just allow open egress to the internet; we need PrivateLink or a managed proxy. how feasible is PrivateLink for your runtime dependencies?
[00:02:20] Jordan: PrivateLink is a strong play if all dependencies can be fronted by endpoints. it avoids NAT egress jitter and keeps traffic inside AWS fabric, but it requires endpoint services and potentially reconfiguring hostnames. tradeoff is cost and operational effort vs NAT with a controlled proxy.
[00:02:40] Samira: note that PrivateLink won't magically fix DNS if you still rely on public resolver paths; you need split-horizon and consistent resolution across AZs. our recommended pattern is private zone with records that map to endpoint ENIs, and then use short TTLs plus a circuit-breaker in the runtime if DNS stalls.
[00:03:05] Marcus: how does the circuit-breaker look in practice?
[00:03:10] Samira: a few pieces: 1) a local stub cache (process-level) for recent name -> ip; 2) a resolver timeout cut-off that fails fast and falls back to the cache; 3) a remote health-check that marks endpoints unhealthy and forces re-resolution; 4) exponential backoff for DNS queries so it doesn't amplify outages. we also track metrics for dns_latency and dns_fail_rate by AZ.
[00:03:40] Jordan: to add to that, we can implement a kernel-level host cache warm-up for known model shard hosts, and a KV cache priming step on startup so first requests aren't waiting on remote name resolution or kv misses.
[00:03:55] Tara: could you describe "kernel-level host cache" — do you mean /etc/hosts entries or a local dnsmasq?
[00:04:05] Diego: both are options. /etc/hosts is static and brittle; dnsmasq or a lightweight stub resolver in each node is more flexible — it gives you a fast cache and control over TTLs. for ephemeral worker fleets we recommend dnsmasq with health-check hooks so you can evict bad entries.
[00:04:25] Alex: what's the recommended TTL for KV cache and DNS for chat workloads where session state matters?
[00:04:33] Samira: for KV cache (session-level), typical is 30s–2m depending on memory hit rate; for DNS we prefer low TTLs (10–30s) but with a warm-up cache so you don't pay the cost on first connection. the low TTL enables quick failover between endpoints.
[00:04:50] Marcus: if we lower the DNS TTL, won't that increase query volume and risk hitting resolver quotas?
[00:04:58] Samira: yes, so the recommended stack is: local stub resolver (reduces queries), circuit-breaker to fail fast, and PrivateLink or internal endpoints to reduce external lookups. plus health-checks to avoid chasing unhealthy endpoints.
[00:05:18] Priya: also from security — we need audit logs for any egress route changes and we need encryption in transit. how does Redwood handle mTLS to a proxy?
[00:05:28] Jordan: our runtime supports configuring an egress proxy with mTLS. you can pin CA bundles and use client certs; we also emit per-request traces and audit events to the console. we'll include sample configs in the playbook.
[00:05:40] Tara: ok, one more network gotcha we hit: NAT scaling causes source port exhaustion sometimes and then packets are dropped intermittently. does PrivateLink avoid that?
[00:05:52] Diego: PrivateLink keeps connections inside and uses ENIs not NAT; so you avoid the NAT port pool exhaustion. it's a primary reason to prefer PrivateLink for high-conn workloads.
[00:06:05] Alex: what about egress through a TLS-terminating proxy that we control? that seems easier than building endpoint services for everything.
[00:06:12] Samira: that's viable. the proxy approach centralizes egress and can provide caching + mTLS. downside is it becomes a single choke point; design it with autoscaling and circuit-breakers. we recommend multiple proxy instances per AZ and health-aware client routing.
[00:06:30] Marcus: pivoting slightly — quantization. we saw some p50 gains but some weird output differences on rare prompts after aggressive 4-bit tuning. any guardrails?
[00:06:42] Jordan: yeah quantization is great for throughput — but have a quality fallback: detect soft-degradation signals (higher repetition, lower log-prob thresholds) and route that inference to a higher-precision variant. Redwood's routing layer can do that automatically if you tag model variants.
[00:06:58] Samira: tie that to your eval set. we'll set up monitors for generation quality metrics and a fallback policy. be mindful that fallback increases cost, so set thresholds conservatively.
[00:07:10] Tara: back to DNS — any suggestions for classic split-horizon mismatch where an internal resolver returns a public IP that isn't reachable from that AZ?
[00:07:20] Diego: we instrumented that before; the fix is to normalize resolution using a resolver placement strategy: use local forwarders that prefer local target addresses in same AZ (EDNS client subnet awareness helps), and ensure private zones map to ENIs via PrivateLink. when inconsistent, the circuit-breaker marks the endpoint unhealthy and forces re-resolve via the other AZ.
[00:07:45] Alex: can you walk through a concrete timeline of an incident and where the circuit-breaker flips?
[00:07:50] Samira: sure — timeline sketch: (1) resolver returns IP -> attempt connect -> SYN retries -> timeout (~300ms); (2) runtime tracks consecutive dns_failures > threshold (eg 3) -> fallback to cache or alternative resolver; (3) mark endpoint unhealthy -> trigger re-resolve -> if re-resolve fails, route to fallback model variant or queue request to other host; (4) emit alert and increase telemetry granularity. the important piece is fail-fast at the DNS layer, not at the application retry layer.
[00:08:35] Marcus: that helps. for reproducing, what logs do you need us to collect?
[00:08:40] Diego: please collect: resolver logs (queries+latency), instance syslogs showing dnsmasq or nscd behavior, NAT gateway metrics (port usage), per-worker runtime traces (dns_latency, connect_latency, kv_miss), and example request ids. we can provide a small logging artifact to ingest into our console.
[00:09:05] Jordan: we'll drop a checklist and the egress playbook link in the follow-up. also we'll include a small repro harness that simulates slow dns to show the circuit-breaker kicking in.
[00:09:17] Tara: great. one more — what about cross-account PrivateLink where endpoint service is managed by a third party? we have services in partner accounts.
[00:09:26] Samira: cross-account PrivateLink works but watch for ENI limits and ensure you expose the right health-checks. also make sure DNS entries in private hosted zones point to the endpoint interface endpoints, not public CNAMEs.
[00:09:45] Alex: ok thanks. let's switch to quick demo of the repro script (Samira)
[00:09:50] Samira: i'll share my screen — small script does repeated resolves, simulates response delay, measures p50/p95 latencies, and shows how the runtime's batch window amplifies tail latency.
[00:10:10] [Screen share/demo for ~20 minutes — internal notes not transcribed verbatim]
[00:30:30] Samira: results: with default batching (max 64) one stalled worker increased p99 from 350ms to ~2.8s; when we reduced max batch to 12 and enabled dns circuit-breaker + stub cache, p99 fell to ~420ms. kv cache priming reduced cold-start tail by ~60%.
[00:31:00] Marcus: good numbers. can you share the repro code and the exact runtime flags used?
[00:31:08] Samira: yes, we'll push repo and flags. also included in playbook: example dnsmasq config, health-check endpoints, and systemd unit for priming job.
[00:31:20] Priya: security checklist — can we run the priming job with least privilege? certificates?
[00:31:26] Diego: yes, priming only needs outbound egress to your endpoints; if you run it inside the private network with mTLS it's just outgoing client cert auth. we provide example RBAC.
[00:31:40] Jordan: wrapping up the recommended phased approach: 1) quick wins — enable stub resolver on hosts, reduce max batch temporarily, priming job; 2) short pilot — route a subset of traffic through PrivateLink or proxy and measure; 3) longer term — full PrivateLink rollout with health-aware routing and quantization quality monitoring.
[00:32:05] Alex: sounds good. next steps?
[00:32:08] Jordan: we'll send the playbook and repro repo; Tara will provide VPC+resolver configs; schedule follow-up week of Jan 5 for results review.
[00:32:20] Marcus: thanks everyone, this was super actionable.
[00:32:24] Jordan: thanks all — we logged action items in the notes. end.
